summary: Asks IANA for a Differentiated Services Code Point for real-time traffic that follows Expedited Forwarding and has been admitted by the network through call admission control. This differs from traffic that is not subject to capacity admission. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a special VIP wristband for voice calls that the network has already said yes to, so they get their reserved space.

subtitle: A second Expedited Forwarding code point that marks voice traffic the network has already agreed to carry.

tldr.problem: Voice calls that the network admitted after checking capacity looked the same on the wire as voice traffic that was never checked, so the network could not give the admitted calls special treatment.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC has IANA assign a second Expedited Forwarding code point, VOICE-ADMIT (101100), for traffic admitted through authentication, authorization and capacity admission. It also recommends admission control for three video classes.
tldr.outcome: Operators can keep admitted and unadmitted real-time traffic apart. The RFC updates RFC 4542 and RFC 4594 and requires capacity admission at the User/Network Interface.

today: RFC 5865 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2010. It updates RFC 4542 and RFC 4594, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: A Second Code Point for Real-Time Traffic
sections.content:
RFC 5865 asks IANA for one Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) for a class of real-time traffic. The class follows the Expedited Forwarding (EF) Per-Hop Behavior from RFC 3246 and RFC 3247, but its traffic is also admitted by the network through a Call Admission Control (CAC) procedure. That procedure involves authentication, authorization and capacity admission.

This differs from real-time EF traffic that has no capacity admission, or only very coarse capacity admission. The new code point applies to the Telephony Service Class described in RFC 4594.

Real-time flows have low tolerance to jitter and loss, and most of them have inelastic flow behavior. Those two traits are what create the need for admission control.
sections.plainLanguage: Some calls need a guaranteed smooth line. This RFC creates a special label for the calls that the network has checked and promised to carry.

sections.title: Key Terms: PHB, DSCP, CAC, UNI and NNI
sections.content:
A Per-Hop Behavior (PHB) is the externally observable forwarding behavior a Differentiated Services node applies to a traffic aggregate. A DSCP is a 6-bit number carried in the 8-bit TOS field of an IPv4 datagram or the Traffic Class field of an IPv6 datagram. Each node uses it to select the PHB for the packet.

Call Admission Control has two parts. Authorization identifies a user, verifies the identity and decides whether the user may use the service. Capacity admission decides whether there is enough capacity for a session's needs under some policy. On the Internet these are separate functions, while in the telephone network they are carried out together with call routing.

A User/Network Interface (UNI) connects two parties that do not trust each other, where the user buys connectivity from the network. UNIs tend to be bottlenecks. A Network/Network Interface (NNI) connects networks that trust each other within limits. NNIs may not be bottlenecks if providers agree to provision excess capacity, but a peering point may have no performance guarantees and may become overloaded.
sections.plainLanguage: The UNI is your front door to the network, where space is tight. The NNI is the gate between two neighboring networks, which usually have more room.

sections.title: The Problem with Unadmitted Voice
sections.content:
The Telephony Service Class in RFC 4594 allows capacity admission, but present implementations either provide none or depend on specific traffic engineering. The edge network relies on engineering by the service provider that might not be present, especially in a mobile environment.

Service providers need to distinguish special-policy traffic from existing Voice over IP services that perform no capacity admission, or only very coarse admission, and can exceed their allocated resources. Agencies want services, such as those described in RFC 4190 and in Section 2.6 of RFC 4504, that treat users differently. That requires capacity admission to separate them from customer-to-customer IP telephony sessions that were not admitted.

The RFC does not add a second code point for video. Instead it recommends, as best practice, admission control for all traffic in three video classes from RFC 4594: Interactive Real-Time Traffic (CS4), Broadcast TV (CS3) when used for video on demand, and AF4 Multimedia Conferencing.
sections.plainLanguage: If everyone's calls look the same, the network cannot tell which ones it promised to protect. A separate label fixes that.

sections.title: Two Ways to Keep Admitted and Unadmitted EF Apart
sections.content:
The RFC describes two data plane designs for isolating the admitted class from ordinary EF. In the multi-priority model, each class has its own policer and its own queue, and the queues have different priorities. Traffic from a higher-priority queue is always sent first, which moves jitter onto the lower-priority queues and gives the higher-priority traffic a smaller average queuing delay. Each queue still needs a policer to protect the network from errors and attacks.

In the multi-policer model, each class is policed to its service level agreement and then all of it feeds one common priority queue. Both classes then see the same jitter, though the combined traffic sees less jitter than elastic traffic in lower-priority queues.

Which is better depends on the traffic. Voice datagrams are small, on the order of 40 to 200 bytes depending on the codec, while video datagrams can be large. On links slower than 10 MBPS, video can add disruptive jitter to voice, so RFC 4594 recommends separate queues at access speeds and RFC 5127 recommends a common queue at optical speeds. If both classes carry the same kind of application, separate policers with a common queue are the better choice.
sections.plainLanguage: You can give the special calls their own fast lane, or put every call in one lane but check each group's ticket first. Which is best depends on what is traveling.

sections.title: Capacity Admission Control Options
sections.content:
The RFC lists six ways capacity admission is done or has been proposed, and notes the weakness of each:

  • Dropping traffic to force sessions to leave. Random loss hits every call and can badly hurt quality on slower links.
  • Admission by assumption or engineering. It depends on assumptions and must be revisited when the network or its usage changes.
  • Call counting. It scales poorly toward the edge of the network.
  • Endpoint probing. The endpoint cannot accurately measure its impact and tends to be greedy.
  • A central bandwidth broker. Central servers lack far-away awareness and real-time reaction.
  • Distributed protocols such as RSVP or NSIS.

For this DSCP the operator's procedure MUST ensure four things: the links a session uses have enough bandwidth, new sessions are refused when bandwidth is inadequate under the relevant policy, a user is identified and the right policy applied, and admission of new sessions does not disrupt existing sessions under stress unless the service explicitly allows it.

The RFC RECOMMENDS a protocol such as RSVP at the UNI, because clear standards do not exist for bandwidth brokers and NSIS is not finalized and is limited to unicast. NNI procedures are business matters between networks and are RECOMMENDED but NOT REQUIRED. Routine and priority calls can share the same DSCP, since which calls are admitted is decided in the control plane, not by data plane policing.
sections.plainLanguage: There are several ways to count how many people fit on a bus. The RFC says the bus must never take on so many that those already aboard get squished, and suggests asking at the door.

sections.title: Changes to RFC 4594
sections.content:
The RFC makes two changes to RFC 4594. First, the Telephony Service Class in RFC 4594 does not involve capacity admission; it relies on application layer admission that only estimates capacity through static engineering. A separate Admitted Telephony Class is added that performs capacity admission dynamically.

Second, capacity admission is added to three video classes: Interactive Real-Time Traffic, Broadcast TV when used for video on demand, and Multimedia Conferencing. The RFC also updates RFC 4542, and points to Section 2.3.5.2 of that RFC for the tools to carry out preemption if it is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: An older rulebook gets two new rules: a new lane for checked voice calls, and a check at the door for three kinds of video.

sections.title: The VOICE-ADMIT Code Point
sections.content:
IANA assigned a DSCP to a second EF traffic class in the Differentiated Services Field Codepoints registry. The class implements the Telephony Service Class at lower speeds and is part of the Real-Time Treatment Aggregate at higher speeds. The value comes from pool 1 and is parallel to the existing EF code point 101110, keeping the first four binary digits the same. The assigned value is 101100, named VOICE-ADMIT.

The traffic class REQUIRES capacity admission, such as RSVP together with AAA services, at the UNI. Use of such services at the NNI is at the option of the interconnected networks.
sections.plainLanguage: EF has a number badge. VOICE-ADMIT gets a badge that looks almost the same, so everyone can tell the two families apart.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The service depends on effective use of a signaling protocol such as RSVP that can identify its user, either an individual or a member of a corporate entity, and assert a policy such as normal, routine or some level of priority. The RFC warns that this capability will be abused if proof of identity is not strong enough or if carriers write or implement policies badly.

Many of the security considerations of RFC 3246, RFC 2474 and RFC 4542 apply. The RFC also points to RFC 4230, which analyzes RSVP, and notes that this document advocates RSVP at the UNI only.
sections.plainLanguage: A special lane is only fair if guards check who is really allowed in. If the check is weak, cheaters will sneak in.
